claim: RIG-I is a key cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that interacts with MAVS to induce type I interferons (IFNs) against RNA virus infection.
source: RIG-I is a key cytosolic pattern recognition receptor that interacts with MAVS to induce type I interferons (IFNs) against RNA virus infection.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of innate immunity, supported by the manuscript's introduction.

claim: Cyclophilin A (CypA) functions as a critical positive regulator of RIG-I-mediated antiviral immune responses.
source: In this study, we found that cyclophilin A (CypA), a peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerase, functioned as a critical positive regulator of RIG-I-mediated antiviral immune responses.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: Deficiency of CypA impaired RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production and promoted viral replication in human cells and mice.
source: Deficiency of CypA impaired RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production and promoted viral replication in human cells and mice.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from CypA-deficient cells and mice shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Upon Sendai virus infection, CypA increased the interaction between RIG-I and its E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM25.
source: Upon Sendai virus infection, CypA increased the interaction between RIG-I and its E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM25, leading to enhanced TRIM25-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I that facilitated recruitment of RIG-I to MAVS.
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 5C and 5D.

claim: CypA enhanced TRIM25-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I that facilitated recruitment of RIG-I to MAVS.
source: Upon Sendai virus infection, CypA increased the interaction between RIG-I and its E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM25, leading to enhanced TRIM25-mediated K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I that facilitated recruitment of RIG-I to MAVS.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assays in Figure 5A and 5B, and mitochondrial fractionation in Figure 5F.

claim: CypA and TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, thereby inhibiting TRIM25-induced K48-linked ubiquitination of MAVS.
source: In addition, CypA and TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, thereby inhibiting TRIM25-induced K48-linked ubiquitination of MAVS.
evidence: Supported by competitive binding experiments in Figure 7F and ubiquitination assays in Figure 7D and 7E.

claim: The innate immune system is the first line of defense against microbial pathogen invasion via the recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) with the help of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs).
source: The innate immune system is the first line of defense against microbial pathogen invasion via the recognition of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) with the help of pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) (Barbalat et al., 2011; Kawai and Akira, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: RIG-I like receptors (RLRs) function as cytoplasmic RNA sensors that recognize viral RNA and activate a signaling pathway essential for the production of type I interferons (IFNs).
source: Among these PRRs, RIG-I like receptors (RLRs) function as cytoplasmic RNA sensors that recognize viral RNA and activate a signaling pathway, which is essential for the production of type I interferons (IFNs) (Kato et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: RIG-I is required for type I IFN production in response to Sendai virus (SeV), Newcastle disease virus (NDV), influenza A virus (IAV), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV).
source: RIG-I is required for type I IFN production in response to Sendai virus (SeV), Newcastle disease virus (NDV), influenza A virus (IAV), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), and Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) (Goubau et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2006; Loo et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Following ligand binding, ubiquitinated RIG-I is recruited to the mitochondria-associated membrane where it binds to MAVS to initiate innate immune signaling.
source: Following ligand binding, ubiquitinated RIG-I is recruited to the mitochondria-associated membrane where it binds to MAVS (also known as IPS-1, Cardif, and VISA) to initiate innate immune signaling (Hou et al., 2011; Kawai et al., 2005; Meylan et al., 2005; Seth et al., 2005; Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cyclophilin A (CypA, encoded by PPIA) is a peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerase (PPIase) that is expressed ubiquitously in all type of cells.
source: Cyclophilin A (CypA, encoded by PPIA) is a peptidyl-prolyl cis/trans isomerase (PPIase) that is expressed ubiquitously in all type of cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CypA.

claim: CypA is the major cellular target for the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA).
source: It is the major cellular target for the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA) and is involved in protein folding, cell signaling, inflammation, and tumorigenesis (Handschumacher et al., 1984; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CypA is involved in protein folding, cell signaling, inflammation, and tumorigenesis.
source: It is the major cellular target for the immunosuppressive drug cyclosporin A (CsA) and is involved in protein folding, cell signaling, inflammation, and tumorigenesis (Handschumacher et al., 1984; Lu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CypA functions as an important host factor that regulates the replication of a number of viruses, including HIV-1, HCV, HPV, IAV, rotavirus, enterovirus-71, and infectious bursal disease virus.
source: Moreover, CypA functions as an important host factor that regulates the replication of a number of viruses, including human immunodeficiency virus type I (HIV-1), hepatitis C virus (HCV), human papillomavirus (HPV), IAV, rotavirus (RV), enterovirus-71 (EV71) virus, and infectious bursal disease virus (IBDV), which expands the role of CypA in virus infection (Bienkowska-Haba et al., 2009; Chatterji et al., 2009; Towers et al., 2003; He et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2012b, 2009; Qing et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CypA interacts directly with viral protein to regulate virus replication.
source: It has been established that CypA interacts directly with viral protein to regulate virus replication.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by examples in the manuscript.

claim: CypA-overexpressing transgenic mice exhibited resistance to influenza A virus infection.
source: For example, our previous studies showed that CypA-overexpressing transgenic mice exhibited resistance to influenza A virus infection (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: CypA interacted with influenza A virus M1 protein and inhibited virus replication by accelerating ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of the M1 protein.
source: We further found that CypA interacted with influenza A virus M1 protein and inhibited virus replication by accelerating ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of the M1 protein (Liu et al., 2012b, 2009; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work by the authors.

claim: CypA can regulate virus replication through modulating host immune responses.
source: Yet several lines of evidence indicate that CypA can also regulate virus replication through modulating host immune responses.
evidence: This is supported by examples and citations in the manuscript.

claim: CypA interacted with the newly synthesized HIV-1 CA domain and subsequently activated the transcription factor IRF3 to promote the production of type I IFNs in dendritic cells.
source: For instance, CypA interacted with the newly synthesized HIV-1 CA domain and subsequently activated the transcription factor IRF3 to promote the production of type I IFNs in dendritic cells (Manel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CypA inhibited rotavirus replication by facilitating IFN-β production.
source: CypA inhibited RV replication by facilitating IFN-β production (He et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The molecular mechanism of how CypA regulates virus-mediated type I IFN production is poorly understood.
source: However, the molecular mechanism of how CypA regulates virus-mediated type I IFN production is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: The hemagglutination (HA) titer of SeV in 293T/CypA- cells was strikingly increased compared with that in 293T/CypA+ cells.
source: The hemagglutination (HA) titer of SeV and median tissue culture infective dose (TCID50) of VSV in 293T/CypA- cells was strikingly increased compared with that in 293T/CypA+ cells (Figure 1A,B), indicating that CypA plays an inhibitory role in the replication of SeV and VSV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The median tissue culture infective dose (TCID50) of VSV in 293T/CypA- cells was strikingly increased compared with that in 293T/CypA+ cells.
source: The hemagglutination (HA) titer of SeV and median tissue culture infective dose (TCID50) of VSV in 293T/CypA- cells was strikingly increased compared with that in 293T/CypA+ cells (Figure 1A,B), indicating that CypA plays an inhibitory role in the replication of SeV and VSV.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CypA plays an inhibitory role in the replication of SeV and VSV.
source: The hemagglutination (HA) titer of SeV and median tissue culture infective dose (TCID50) of VSV in 293T/CypA- cells was strikingly increased compared with that in 293T/CypA+ cells (Figure 1A,B), indicating that CypA plays an inhibitory role in the replication of SeV and VSV.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing increased viral titers in CypA-deficient cells.

claim: The mRNA expression level of SeV M gene was higher in Ppia−/− BMDMs than that in WT BMDMs.
source: Consistent with the results in 293T cells, we found that the mRNA expression level of SeV M gene was higher in Ppia−/− BMDMs than that in WT BMDMs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: CypA inhibited the replication of RIG-I-recognized RNA viruses.
source: Collectively, these data suggested that CypA inhibited the replication of RIG-I-recognized RNA viruses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: Absence of CypA remarkably decreased RIG-I-mediated production of type I IFNs and ISGs.
source: Absence of CypA remarkably decreased RIG-I-mediated production of type I IFNs and ISGs.
evidence: Supported by luciferase assays, quantitative PCR, and ELISA data shown in Figure 1D-G.

claim: CypA positively regulated expression of type I IFNs and ISGs against RIG-I-recognized RNA virus infection.
source: Collectively, these findings suggested that CypA positively regulated expression of type I IFNs and ISGs against RIG-I-recognized RNA virus infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results showing decreased IFN production in CypA-deficient cells.

claim: CypA promoted IFN-β and ISGs production and inhibited the replication of EMCV.
source: CypA promoted IFN-β and ISGs production and inhibited the replication of EMCV (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), but had no impact on HSV-1-triggered cGAS-STING pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: CypA had no impact on HSV-1-triggered cGAS-STING pathway.
source: CypA promoted IFN-β and ISGs production and inhibited the replication of EMCV (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B), but had no impact on HSV-1-triggered cGAS-STING pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: CypA was highly inducible upon virus infection.
source: When we investigated the mRNA and protein levels of CypA in BMDMs, 293T cells, U937 cells and human monocytes infected with SeV, VSV or IAV-mut, we found that CypA was highly inducible, whereas Poly (I:C) transfection or IFN-β treatment made no difference to CypA expression, (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting that the induction of CypA can be triggered by viruses and CypA is involved in cellular antiviral response.
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-D.

claim: Poly (I:C) transfection or IFN-β treatment made no difference to CypA expression.
source: When we investigated the mRNA and protein levels of CypA in BMDMs, 293T cells, U937 cells and human monocytes infected with SeV, VSV or IAV-mut, we found that CypA was highly inducible, whereas Poly (I:C) transfection or IFN-β treatment made no difference to CypA expression, (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting that the induction of CypA can be triggered by viruses and CypA is involved in cellular antiviral response.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A-D.

claim: The induction of CypA can be triggered by viruses.
source: When we investigated the mRNA and protein levels of CypA in BMDMs, 293T cells, U937 cells and human monocytes infected with SeV, VSV or IAV-mut, we found that CypA was highly inducible, whereas Poly (I:C) transfection or IFN-β treatment made no difference to CypA expression, (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting that the induction of CypA can be triggered by viruses and CypA is involved in cellular antiviral response.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that virus infection, but not Poly(I:C) or IFN-β, induces CypA expression.

claim: CypA is involved in cellular antiviral response.
source: When we investigated the mRNA and protein levels of CypA in BMDMs, 293T cells, U937 cells and human monocytes infected with SeV, VSV or IAV-mut, we found that CypA was highly inducible, whereas Poly (I:C) transfection or IFN-β treatment made no difference to CypA expression, (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A–D), suggesting that the induction of CypA can be triggered by viruses and CypA is involved in cellular antiviral response.
evidence: This is inferred from the virus-induced expression of CypA and its effects on viral replication and IFN production.

claim: Upon virus infection, CypA expression was upregulated, which inhibited the replication RIG-I-recognized RNA virus by enhancing production of type I IFNs.
source: Taken together, upon virus infection, CypA expression was upregulated, which inhibited the replication RIG-I-recognized RNA virus by enhancing production of type I IFNs.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 1.

claim: All five monitored SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice died at 9 d after infection, whereas three of five (60%) SeV-infected WT mice survived.
source: In a mouse model of SeV infection, all five monitored SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice died at 9 d after infection, whereas three of five (60%) SeV-infected WT mice survived and remained healthy for the duration of the infection study (Figure 2A), indicating deficiency of CypA accelerated SeV infection-induced death of mice.
evidence: Supported by survival data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Deficiency of CypA accelerated SeV infection-induced death of mice.
source: In a mouse model of SeV infection, all five monitored SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice died at 9 d after infection, whereas three of five (60%) SeV-infected WT mice survived and remained healthy for the duration of the infection study (Figure 2A), indicating deficiency of CypA accelerated SeV infection-induced death of mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the survival data showing all CypA-deficient mice died while 60% of WT mice survived.

claim: SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice exhibited much higher lung indices than that of WT mice.
source: Anatomical analysis showed that the lung indices of SeV-infected mice were increased at 7 d after infection. Notably, SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice exhibited much higher lung indices than that of WT mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by lung index measurements shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gross lesion of lung in Ppia−/− mice infected with SeV was severer than that in WT mice.
source: Consistently, gross lesion of lung in Ppia−/− mice infected with SeV was severer than that in WT mice (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by gross pathology images shown in Figure 2C.

claim: SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice displayed severe bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, congestion in blood vessels, and dropout of the mucous epithelium.
source: We further performed histopathological examination of lung, nasal turbinate, and trachea tissues at day 2, 5 and 7 post infection and found that SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice displayed severe bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, congestion in blood vessels, and dropout of the mucous epithelium, whereas SeV-infected WT mice only displayed slight bronchopneumonia and congestion in blood vessels during the infection (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by histopathological examination shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: SeV-infected WT mice only displayed slight bronchopneumonia and congestion in blood vessels during the infection.
source: We further performed histopathological examination of lung, nasal turbinate, and trachea tissues at day 2, 5 and 7 post infection and found that SeV-infected Ppia−/− mice displayed severe bronchopneumonia, interstitial pneumonia, congestion in blood vessels, and dropout of the mucous epithelium, whereas SeV-infected WT mice only displayed slight bronchopneumonia and congestion in blood vessels during the infection (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by histopathological examination shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Tissue damage was aggravated in CypA deficient mice, correlating with a higher viral load in the lungs.
source: These data showed that tissue damage was aggravated in CypA deficient mice, correlating with a higher viral load in the lungs, as measured by expression of NP and M genes of SeV (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by viral gene expression data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deficiency of CypA reduced expression of type I IFNs and downstream ISGs in lungs and spleens.
source: Most importantly, we found deficiency of CypA reduced expression of type I IFNs and downstream ISGs in lungs (Figure 2F–H) and spleens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that CypA also promoted type I IFN production in vivo.
evidence: Supported by ELISA and quantitative PCR data shown in Figure 2F-H and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: CypA promoted type I IFN production in vivo.
source: Most importantly, we found deficiency of CypA reduced expression of type I IFNs and downstream ISGs in lungs (Figure 2F–H) and spleens (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D), suggesting that CypA also promoted type I IFN production in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced IFN expression in CypA-deficient mice.

claim: CypA inhibited SeV replication in vivo through augmenting of expression of IFNs and downstream ISGs.
source: Collectively, CypA inhibited SeV replication in vivo through augmenting of expression of IFNs and downstream ISGs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the in vivo experimental results in Figure 2.

claim: Expression of type I IFN genes is mainly regulated by two transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB.
source: It is well established that expression of type I IFN genes is mainly regulated by two transcription factors IRF3 and NF-κB.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field of innate immunity.

claim: ISRE- and NF-κB-responsive luciferase activity induced by SeV infection were dramatically lower in the absence of CypA.
source: We found that ISRE- and NF-κB-responsive luciferase activity induced by SeV infection were dramatically lower in the absence of CypA (Figure 3A,B), indicating that CypA was involved in both IRF3- and NF-κB-mediated type I IFN expression.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: CypA was involved in both IRF3- and NF-κB-mediated type I IFN expression.
source: We found that ISRE- and NF-κB-responsive luciferase activity induced by SeV infection were dramatically lower in the absence of CypA (Figure 3A,B), indicating that CypA was involved in both IRF3- and NF-κB-mediated type I IFN expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced luciferase activity in CypA-deficient cells.

claim: The activated dimer form of IRF3 and phosphorylation of IRF3 and p65 were distinctly suppressed in SeV-infected 293T/CypA- cells compared with those in SeV-infected 293T/CypA+ cells.
source: In line with this observation, the activated dimer form of IRF3 (Figure 3C) and phosphorylation of IRF3 and p65 (Figure 3D) were distinctly suppressed in SeV-infected 293T/CypA- cells compared with those in SeV-infected 293T/CypA+ cells.
evidence: Supported by native PAGE and Western blot data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: CypA deficiency inhibited phosphorylation of IRF3, p65, IKKα/β, and IκBα in cultured BMDMs.
source: Moreover, CypA deficiency also inhibited phosphorylation of IRF3, p65, IKKα/β, and IκBα in cultured BMDMs, accompanied with lower expression levels of RIG-I and MAVS (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: CypA is vital for activation of IRF3 and NF-κB signaling pathways.
source: These data indicate that CypA is vital for activation of IRF3 and NF-κB signaling pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 3.

claim: CypA promoted the activation of the IFN-β promoter, ISRE and NF-κB induced by overexpression of RIG-I-N, MDA5-N, and MAVS, but not induced by TBK1 or IRF3/5D.
source: We found that CypA promoted the activation of the IFN-β promoter (Figure 4A), ISRE (Figure 4B) and NF-κB (Figure 4C) induced by overexpression of RIG-I-N, MDA5-N, and MAVS, but not induced by TBK1 or IRF3/5D, suggesting that RIG-I, MDA5, and MAVS were involved in CypA-regulated RLR pathway.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: RIG-I, MDA5, and MAVS were involved in CypA-regulated RLR pathway.
source: We found that CypA promoted the activation of the IFN-β promoter (Figure 4A), ISRE (Figure 4B) and NF-κB (Figure 4C) induced by overexpression of RIG-I-N, MDA5-N, and MAVS, but not induced by TBK1 or IRF3/5D, suggesting that RIG-I, MDA5, and MAVS were involved in CypA-regulated RLR pathway.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of CypA on different pathway components.

claim: CypA increased the dimerization of IRF3 induced by overexpression of RIG-I, MDA5 and MAVS.
source: Consistent with these findings, CypA increased the dimerization of IRF3 induced by overexpression of RIG-I, MDA5 and MAVS (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by native PAGE data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CypA interacted with the transfected RIG-I, MDA5, or MAVS in 293T cells.
source: Coimmunoprecipitation assay did show that CypA interacted with the transfected RIG-I, MDA5, or MAVS in 293T cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Endogenous CypA-RIG-I interaction and CypA-MAVS interaction occurred in SeV-infected conditions.
source: We further observed the endogenous CypA-RIG-I interaction and CypA-MAVS interaction in SeV-infected conditions (Figure 4F,G).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4F,G.

claim: CypA co-localized with the endogenous RIG-I and MAVS in 293T cells after infection with SeV.
source: Confocal microscopy experiments indicated that CypA co-localized with the endogenous RIG-I and MAVS in 293T cells after infection with SeV (Figure 4H), which are consistent with the results of Figure 4F,G, indicating that RIG-I and MAVS were the target proteins of CypA to augment RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: RIG-I and MAVS were the target proteins of CypA to augment RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production.
source: Confocal microscopy experiments indicated that CypA co-localized with the endogenous RIG-I and MAVS in 293T cells after infection with SeV (Figure 4H), which are consistent with the results of Figure 4F,G, indicating that RIG-I and MAVS were the target proteins of CypA to augment RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production.
evidence: This is inferred from the interaction and colocalization data.

claim: Following ligand binding, RIG-I is ubiquitinated by the E3 ligase TRIM25.
source: Following ligand binding, RIG-I is ubiquitinated by the E3 ligase TRIM25.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Transfected CypA enhanced exogenous TRIM25-mediated K63-linked, but not K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I.
source: In 293T/CypA- cells, transfected CypA enhanced exogenous TRIM25-mediated K63-linked, but not K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I (Figure 5A) and increased the interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: CypA increased the interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I.
source: In 293T/CypA- cells, transfected CypA enhanced exogenous TRIM25-mediated K63-linked, but not K48-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I (Figure 5A) and increased the interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Endogenous ubiquitination of RIG-I and endogenous interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I were enhanced by CypA in BMDMs upon SeV infection.
source: Furthermore, we observed similar results of endogenous ubiquitination of RIG-I and endogenous interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I in BMDMs upon SeV infection (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: TRIM25 interacts with RIG-I-N to deliver the Lys 63-linked ubiquitin to the CARDs of RIG-I.
source: It is well known that TRIM25 interacts with RIG-I-N to deliver the Lys 63-linked ubiquitin to the CARDs of RIG-I (Gack et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CypA interacted with RIG-I-C (C-terminal of RIG-I).
source: We performed coimmunoprecipitation assays to explore the CypA-binding region of RIG-I. We found that the CypA interacted with RIG-I-C (C-terminal of RIG-I) (Figure 5E), indicating that CypA and TRIM25 bind to different regions of RIG-I.
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CypA and TRIM25 bind to different regions of RIG-I.
source: We performed coimmunoprecipitation assays to explore the CypA-binding region of RIG-I. We found that the CypA interacted with RIG-I-C (C-terminal of RIG-I) (Figure 5E), indicating that CypA and TRIM25 bind to different regions of RIG-I.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that CypA binds RIG-I-C while TRIM25 is known to bind RIG-I-N.

claim: RIG-I induction was strongly decreased and much less RIG-I was found in mitochondria of BMDMs when CypA was absent.
source: We observed that RIG-I induction was strongly decreased and much less RIG-I was found in mitochondria of BMDMs when CypA was absent (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation and Western blot data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CypA promoted RIG-I induction and facilitated recruitment of RIG-I to mitochondria upon SeV infection.
source: The results confirmed that CypA promoted RIG-I induction and facilitated recruitment of RIG-I to mitochondria upon SeV infection (Figure 5G), which are consistent with the results of Figure 5F.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: CypA enhanced RIG-I-MAVS interaction.
source: We then investigated the effect of CypA on the interaction between RIG-I and MAVS. Coimmunoprecipitation experiment indicated that CypA enhanced RIG-I-MAVS interaction (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: CypA was detected in mitochondria and its expression level was upregulated both in mitochondria and cytoplasm against SeV infection.
source: More interestingly, aside from the well-known cytoplasmic distribution (Galat and Metcalfe, 1995), CypA was also detected in mitochondria and its expression level was upregulated both in mitochondria and cytoplasm against SeV infection (Figure 5F), a finding confirmed by an immunofluorescence assay in 293T/CypA+ cells (Figure 5I), suggesting that CypA plays important roles in response to virus infection both in mitochondria and cytoplasm.
evidence: Supported by subcellular fractionation data shown in Figure 5F and confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: CypA plays important roles in response to virus infection both in mitochondria and cytoplasm.
source: More interestingly, aside from the well-known cytoplasmic distribution (Galat and Metcalfe, 1995), CypA was also detected in mitochondria and its expression level was upregulated both in mitochondria and cytoplasm against SeV infection (Figure 5F), a finding confirmed by an immunofluorescence assay in 293T/CypA+ cells (Figure 5I), suggesting that CypA plays important roles in response to virus infection both in mitochondria and cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization and upregulation of CypA in both compartments upon infection.

claim: Upon SeV infection, CypA increased the interaction between the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM25 and RIG-I and promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I to facilitate recruitment of RIG-I to MAVS, leading to up-regulation of RIG-I signaling pathway.
source: Taken together, upon SeV infection, CypA increased the interaction between the E3 ubiquitin ligase TRIM25 and RIG-I and promoted K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I to facilitate recruitment of RIG-I to MAVS, leading to up-regulation of RIG-I signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 5.

claim: CypA inhibited the degradation of exogenous MAVS, but had no effect on the stability of exogenous RIG-I and MDA5.
source: The western blotting result showed that CypA inhibited the degradation of exogenous MAVS, but had no effect on the stability of exogenous RIG-I and MDA5 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: CypA enhanced the stability of endogenous MAVS without or with SeV infection.
source: Also, CypA enhanced the stability of endogenous MAVS without or with SeV infection (Figure 6B,C).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: CypA plays a key role in stabilizing MAVS.
source: These data indicated that CypA plays key a role in stabilizing MAVS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stability assay results.

claim: The proteasome inhibitor MG132 significantly inhibited the degradation of MAVS, whereas the lysosome inhibitor NH4Cl did not.
source: In 293T/CypA+ and 293T/CypA- cells, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 significantly inhibited the degradation of MAVS, whereas the lysosome inhibitor NH4Cl did not (Figure 6D), indicating that the degradation of MAVS is controlled by ubiquitin-meditated proteolysis.
evidence: Supported by inhibitor treatment data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The degradation of MAVS is controlled by ubiquitin-meditated proteolysis.
source: In 293T/CypA+ and 293T/CypA- cells, the proteasome inhibitor MG132 significantly inhibited the degradation of MAVS, whereas the lysosome inhibitor NH4Cl did not (Figure 6D), indicating that the degradation of MAVS is controlled by ubiquitin-meditated proteolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the selective effect of proteasome but not lysosome inhibitor.

claim: MAVS ubiquitination was inhibited in the presence of CypA.
source: We further investigated the effects of CypA on MAVS ubiquitination. MAVS ubiquitination was inhibited in the presence of CypA (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: CypA significantly decreased the ubiquitination of MAVS.
source: Consistently, in coimmunoprecipitation experiments, we also found that CypA significantly decreased the ubiquitination of MAVS (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The absence of CypA accelerated the degradation of MAVS amino acids 360–540, while substitutions K371A and K420A completely withstood the degradation.
source: The absence of CypA accelerated the degradation of MAVS amino acids 360–540, while substitutions K371A and K420A completely withstood the degradation (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: CypA suppressed ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation of MAVS.
source: Together, CypA suppressed ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation of MAVS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ubiquitination and degradation assay results.

claim: E3 ubiquitin ligases TRIM25, Smurf1, Smurf2, AIP4, RNF5, and RNF125 have been shown to mediate K48-ubiquitination and degradation of MAVS.
source: E3 ubiquitin ligases TRIM25, Smurf1, Smurf2, AIP4, RNF5, and RNF125 have been shown to mediate K48-ubiquitination and degradation of MAVS (Arimoto et al., 2007; Castanier et al., 2012; Pan et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2012; You et al., 2009; Zhong et al., 2010), so it is important to identify the specific ubiquitin ligase involved in CypA-regulated MAVS ubiquitination.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CypA increased the expression of IFN-β in the presence of TRIM25 and Smurf1 but not with AIP4, RNF125 and RNF5.
source: The luciferase assay indicated that CypA increased the expression of IFN-β in the presence of TRIM25 and Smurf1 but not with AIP4, RNF125 and RNF5 (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: The level of endogenous MAVS protein was considerably increased in TRIM25 and CypA co-expressing cells compared with cells only transfected with TRIM25.
source: We found that the level of endogenous MAVS protein was considerably increased in TRIM25 and CypA co-expressing cells compared with cells only transfected with TRIM25, suggesting that CypA inhibits TRIM25-mediated MAVS degradation (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CypA inhibits TRIM25-mediated MAVS degradation.
source: We found that the level of endogenous MAVS protein was considerably increased in TRIM25 and CypA co-expressing cells compared with cells only transfected with TRIM25, suggesting that CypA inhibits TRIM25-mediated MAVS degradation (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased MAVS protein level in the presence of both CypA and TRIM25.

claim: The ubiquitination of MAVS was inhibited in TRIM25 and CypA co-expressing cells compared with that transfected with TRIM25.
source: In accordance with the stability assay, the ubiquitination of MAVS was inhibited in TRIM25 and CypA co-expressing cells compared with that transfected with TRIM25 (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: CypA almost had no effect on Smurf1-mediated MAVS stability and ubiquitination.
source: However, CypA almost had no effect on Smurf1-mediated MAVS stability and ubiquitination (Figure 7B,C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7B,C.

claim: CypA could enhance the TRIM25-mediated K48-linked, but not K63-linked ubiquitination of both exogenous and endogenous MAVS.
source: Furthermore, we observed that CypA could enhance the TRIM25-mediated K48-linked, but not K63-linked ubiquitination of both exogenous and endogenous MAVS (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: CypA-MAVS interaction was reduced in the presence of TRIM25.
source: CypA-MAVS interaction was reduced in the presence of TRIM25, and TRIM25-MAVS interaction also reduced in the presence of CypA (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: TRIM25-MAVS interaction was reduced in the presence of CypA.
source: CypA-MAVS interaction was reduced in the presence of TRIM25, and TRIM25-MAVS interaction also reduced in the presence of CypA (Figure 7F).
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: CypA and TRIM25 both bind to MAVS amino acids 360–540.
source: Just as we speculated, CypA (Figure 7G) and TRIM25 (Figure 7H) both bind to MAVS amino acids 360–540.
evidence: Supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7G,H.

claim: CypA and the E3 ligase TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, thereby inhibiting ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation of MAVS.
source: Thus, our results indicated that CypA and the E3 ligase TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, thereby inhibiting ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation of MAVS.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the competitive binding and ubiquitination data.

claim: TRIM25 targets MAVS at K7 and K10 for ubiquitination.
source: It has been reported that TRIM25 targets MAVS at K7 and K10 for ubiquitination and AIP4 mediates MAVS ubiquitination at K371 and K420 (Castanier et al., 2012; You et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AIP4 mediates MAVS ubiquitination at K371 and K420.
source: It has been reported that TRIM25 targets MAVS at K7 and K10 for ubiquitination and AIP4 mediates MAVS ubiquitination at K371 and K420 (Castanier et al., 2012; You et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Both the MAVS mutation KK-AA (with the substitutions K371A and K420A) and KK-RR (with the substitutions K7R and K10R) distinctly reduced MAVS ubiquitination.
source: Both the MAVS mutation KK-AA (with the substitutions K371A and K420A) and KK-RR (with the substitutions K7R and K10R) distinctly reduced MAVS ubiquitination (Figure 7I), suggesting that K371 and K420, as well as K7 and K10, are the ubiquitination sites for TRIM25-mediated MAVS ubiquitination.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: K371 and K420, as well as K7 and K10, are the ubiquitination sites for TRIM25-mediated MAVS ubiquitination.
source: Both the MAVS mutation KK-AA (with the substitutions K371A and K420A) and KK-RR (with the substitutions K7R and K10R) distinctly reduced MAVS ubiquitination (Figure 7I), suggesting that K371 and K420, as well as K7 and K10, are the ubiquitination sites for TRIM25-mediated MAVS ubiquitination.
evidence: This is inferred from the reduced ubiquitination when these residues are mutated.

claim: CypA and TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, which inhibited TRIM25-mediated MAVS ubiquitination at K371 and K420.
source: Collectively, CypA and TRIM25 competitively interacted with MAVS, which inhibited TRIM25-mediated MAVS ubiquitination at K371 and K420.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the experimental results in Figure 7.

claim: CypA has been shown to interact with p65 and inhibit the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of p65, thereby promoting innate immune responses.
source: CypA has been shown to interact with p65 and inhibit the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of p65, thereby promoting innate immune responses (Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CypA increased IFN-β expression and IRF3/p65 phosphorylation with the treatment of overexpressed RIG-I and MAVS respectively.
source: CypA increased IFN-β expression and IRF3/p65 phosphorylation with the treatment of overexpressed RIG-I and MAVS respectively (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: CypA still had impact on IFN-β expression and IRF3 phosphorylation when 293T/RIG-I−/− were transfected with Flag-RIG-I and treated with BAY-11–7082, or when 293T/RIG-I−/− were transfected with Flag-MAVS and treated with BAY-11–7082.
source: We found that CypA still had impact on IFN-β expression and IRF3 phosphorylation when 293T/RIG-I−/− were transfected with Flag-RIG-I and treated with BAY-11–7082, or when 293T/RIG-I−/− were transfected with Flag-MAVS and treated with BAY-11–7082 (Figure 7J).
evidence: Supported by quantitative PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 7J.

claim: CypA is able to promote type I IFN production at the level of RIG-I and MAVS, which is independent of the downstream p65.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that CypA is able to promote type I IFN production at the level of RIG-I and MAVS, which is independent of the downstream p65.
evidence: This is inferred from the persistence of CypA effects even when NF-κB is inhibited.

claim: CypA could inhibit SeV replication by regulating RIG-I- and MAVS-directed type I IFN production.
source: Accordingly, CypA could inhibit SeV replication by regulating RIG-I- and MAVS-directed type I IFN production (Figure 7K).
evidence: Supported by viral replication assay data shown in Figure 7K.

claim: CypA was highly induced in human gastric carcinoma cell line upon H9N2 influenza virus infection.
source: It had been reported that CypA was highly induced in human gastric carcinoma cell line upon H9N2 influenza virus infection by using proteomics analysis (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CypA participates in cellular antiviral response.
source: We also found that CypA was inducible in BMDMs, 293T cells, U937 cells and human monocytes infected by SeV, VSV or IAV-mut, indicating that CypA participates in cellular antiviral response.
evidence: This is inferred from the induction of CypA upon viral infection.

claim: The ubiquitin system has been certified to play an essential role in precisely controlling RIG-I-mediated signal transduction.
source: The ubiquitin system has been certified to play an essential role in precisely controlling RIG-I-mediated signal transduction (Heaton et al., 2016; Maelfait and Beyaert, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Upon RNA virus infection, viral RNA bind to RIG-I followed by the binding of TRIM25 to deliver the K63 ubiquitin chains to RIG-I.
source: Upon RNA virus infection, viral RNA bind to RIG-I followed by the binding of TRIM25 to deliver the K63 ubiquitin chains to RIG-I (Gack et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2012; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Peisley et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016), then the CARD domains of RIG-I are exposed to interact with the CARD domains of MAVS.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The CARD domains of RIG-I are exposed to interact with the CARD domains of MAVS after K63 ubiquitination.
source: Upon RNA virus infection, viral RNA bind to RIG-I followed by the binding of TRIM25 to deliver the K63 ubiquitin chains to RIG-I (Gack et al., 2007; Jiang et al., 2012; Kowalinski et al., 2011; Peisley et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016), then the CARD domains of RIG-I are exposed to interact with the CARD domains of MAVS.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 14-3-3ε is essential for the stable interaction of RIG-I with TRIM25, which facilitates RIG-I ubiquitination and initiation of innate immunity against hepatitis C virus and other pathogenic RNA viruses.
source: It has also been reported that another RIG-I binding protein, 14-3-3ε, is essential for the stable interaction of RIG-I with TRIM25, which facilitates RIG-I ubiquitination and initiation of innate immunity against hepatitis C virus and other pathogenic RNA viruses. (Liu et al., 2012a).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CypA could be defined as a key mitochondrial targeting chaperone protein that is required for innate antiviral responses.
source: Therefore, just like 14-3-3ε, CypA could be defined as a key mitochondrial targeting chaperone protein that is required for innate antiviral responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of CypA's function to that of 14-3-3ε.

claim: MAVS undergoes K48-linked ubiquitination during virus infection, which mediates MAVS degradation.
source: It has been established that MAVS undergoes K48-linked ubiquitination during virus infection, which mediates MAVS degradation (Liu et al., 2013; Paz et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some host proteins, including PCBP2, IRTKS and Ndfip1, promoted E3 ligase AIP4- or Smurf-mediated MAVS ubiquitination for degradation, leading to suppressed type I IFN production.
source: A number of studies have showed that some host proteins, including PCBP2, IRTKS and Ndfip1, promoted E3 ligase AIP4- or Smurf-mediated MAVS ubiquitination for degradation, leading to suppressed type I IFN production (Wang et al., 2012; Xia et al., 2015; You et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inhibition of MAVS degradation facilitated RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production.
source: All these data indicated that inhibition of MAVS degradation facilitated RIG-I-mediated type I IFN production.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that CypA inhibits MAVS degradation and enhances IFN production.

claim: The proteasomal degradation of MAVS was required to release the signaling complex into the cytosol for phosphorylation of IRF3 and subsequent production of IFN-β.
source: However, a previous study suggested that the proteasomal degradation of MAVS was required to release the signaling complex into the cytosol for phosphorylation of IRF3 and subsequent production of IFN-β (Castanier et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature that is cited but questioned by the authors.

claim: CypA accelerates ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of the M1 protein of influenza virus and then restricts virus replication.
source: Besides CypA-regulated ubiquitination of RIG-I and MAVS, we have reported that CypA accelerates ubiquitin-proteasome degradation of the M1 protein of influenza virus and then restricts virus replication(Liu et al., 2012b).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: CypA and Pin1 both enhance the stability of P65 by blocking the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, and SOCS-1 is the ubiquitin ligase for P65.
source: Additionally, CypA and another PPIase, Pin1, both enhance the stability of P65 by blocking the ubiquitin-proteasome degradation, and SOCS-1 is the ubiquitin ligase for P65 (Ryo et al., 2003; Sun et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PPIases have some common function in regulating ubiquitination of proteins.
source: These results support the hypothesis that PPIases have some common function in regulating ubiquitination of proteins.
evidence: This is a hypothesis inferred from the similar functions of CypA and Pin1.

claim: CypA controls RIG-I-mediated antiviral immune responses through a ubiquitination-based mechanism.
source: Together, we reveal a ubiquitination-based mechanism by which CypA controls RIG-I-mediated antiviral immune responses.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the findings.

claim: CypA is widely distributed in almost all tissues.
source: CypA is widely distributed in almost all tissues.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CypA.

claim: CypA interacts with a large number of proteins and plays various biological roles through different mechanisms.
source: Multiple lines of evidence have revealed that CypA interacts with a large number of proteins and plays various biological roles through different mechanisms.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CypA.

claim: The conformation of RIG-I-N might be changed as soon as CypA interacted with RIG-I-C, then the binding site of TRIM25 was exposed, which facilitated the interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I-N.
source: We speculated that the conformation of RIG-I-N might be changed as soon as CypA interacted with RIG-I-C, then the binding site of TRIM25 was exposed, which facilitated the interaction between TRIM25 and RIG-I-N.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed by the authors to explain their observations.

claim: CypA regulates RIG-I signaling in two ways: promoting K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I and recruiting more RIG-I to MAVS, and stabilizing MAVS by suppressing its ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation.
source: In conclusion, our data demonstrated that CypA regulates RIG-I signaling in two ways. On one hand, CypA promotes K63-linked ubiquitination of RIG-I and recruits more RIG-I to MAVS. On the other hand, CypA stabilizes MAVS by suppressing its ubiquitin-mediated proteasome degradation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, summarizing the two mechanisms identified.

claim: The findings expand the biological functions of CypA in RIG-I-mediated antiviral innate immunity and provide a potential novel target for manipulating viral infection.
source: Hence, our data further expand the biological functions of CypA in RIG-I-mediated antiviral innate immunity and provide a potential novel target for manipulating viral infection.
evidence: This is a concluding statement about the implications of the study.
